lines.text: One of the oldest nations on Earth, home to great empires, poets and a revolution that shook the world. This is the story of Iran.
It begins in the south-west with Elam, ruled from Susa, a rival of Mesopotamia for two thousand years with a language and writing of its own.
Around 1250 BCE the Elamites raised the great ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil, still standing on the plain today.
In these lands arose Zoroastrianism, a faith of the god Ahura Mazda and the struggle of truth against falsehood, still kept in Iran and by India's Parsis.
Then came Cyrus the Great, who conquered the Medes, Lydia and Babylon, and let his peoples keep their own customs and faiths.
His Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to the Indus, held together by governors, a royal road and tolerance.
Its first capital was Pasargadae, where Cyrus himself lies buried in a simple stone tomb.
Later kings built Persepolis on a mountain terrace, its stairways carved with peoples from across the empire bearing gifts.
From that ancient world comes Nowruz, the new year kept at the spring equinox, still celebrated by millions across Iran and its neighbours.
After Alexander, the Parthians took Persia. Their mounted archers crushed a Roman army at Carrhae, and they held the trade roads for five centuries.
The Sasanians followed, the last great Persian empire before Islam, rivals of Rome, with Zoroastrianism as their faith and a court famed for silver and silk.
After the Arab conquest brought Islam, Persian culture rose again. Ferdowsi spent decades on the Shahnameh, the epic that kept the Persian language alive.
Avicenna, the physician and philosopher, wrote a Canon of Medicine used as a textbook in the Islamic world and in Europe for centuries.
From Shiraz came Saadi, whose lines on the unity of all people are written today at the United Nations.
And Hafez, also of Shiraz, wrote lyrics of love, wine and longing. Many Iranians keep his book at home and open it to read their future.
In 1501 Shah Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty and made Shia Islam the faith of the state, as it is to this day.
Under the Safavids the Iran we know took shape, a country on its high plateau, the heart of old Persia.
Shah Abbas made Isfahan his capital and laid out its great square, Naqsh-e Jahan, framed by mosques and palaces.
Centuries later, Mohammad Mosaddegh would become prime minister, take Iran's oil into national hands, and be overthrown for it.
Ruhollah Khomeini, a Shia cleric, would one day lead a revolution and become the first Supreme Leader of an Islamic Republic.
In 1905 a revolution began that won Iran its first parliament, an early step toward government by the people.
Mohammad Reza Pahlavi would be the last shah, ruling from 1941 until the revolution swept him away.
His father, Reza Shah, founded the Pahlavi dynasty in 1925, and set out to modernise Iran, often by force.
Ali Khamenei would succeed Khomeini in 1989 and hold the power of Supreme Leader for more than three decades.
In 1953 a coup backed by Britain and the United States removed Mosaddegh, and left a bitterness that still shapes Iran's politics.
In 1978 mass protests rose against the Shah. Within months he was gone, Khomeini was back, and Iran became an Islamic Republic.
Students seized the American embassy in Tehran and held fifty-two Americans for four hundred and forty-four days.
Then Iraq invaded. The war lasted eight years, with trench fighting and chemical weapons, and ended with the borders almost unchanged.
In 2011 Asghar Farhadi's film A Separation won the Oscar, showing the world the everyday lives of Iranian families.
In 2015 a deal was struck to limit Iran's nuclear programme in return for lifting sanctions.
In 2022 a young woman, Mahsa Amini, died in police custody, and women led protests that spread across the country.
And in June 2025 came a twelve-day war, as Israel and the United States struck Iran's nuclear sites and Iran fired missiles at Israel.
From Elam to the Islamic Republic, Iran's long story is far from over.
